text: A notebook is a wonderful place to explore and a terrible place to hide mistakes. The same notebook that took you an hour to write can take a colleague, or you next month, two hours to understand. Clean code isn't about style points — it's about making your analysis something other people, including future you, can read, trust, and rerun. This lesson applies a small set of habits that make the biggest difference for the least effort.

Look at this calculation on a tiny illustrative orders table. Nobody can tell what s, q, p, or 0.92 are actually supposed to mean. Worse, this exact code triggers pandas' SettingWithCopyWarning, because x is a slice of d, and we then assign a brand-new column straight into that slice — exactly the gotcha from Chapter 3.

Here's the cleaned-up version. The magic number 0.92 became a named constant, LOYALTY underscore DISCOUNT, with a comment explaining exactly why it's 0.92. The logic moved into a function, add underscore order underscore total, with a one-line docstring, that copies its input with dot-copy before changing anything, so it never mutates the caller's original data. Running it on three completed orders prints order totals of 18.4, 23.0, and 18.4 — same math, completely readable now.

If you've pasted the same five lines into three different cells, you have a function waiting to be written. A good notebook function does exactly one job, takes its inputs as arguments rather than quietly reading a global DataFrame defined somewhere in an earlier cell, returns its result instead of mutating anything in place, and carries a one-line docstring. That hidden dependency on an earlier cell's variable is exactly what breaks the moment cells run out of order.

Notebooks let you run cells in any order, and the kernel remembers everything regardless of that order — that's the source of the classic it-worked-yesterday bug. A variable you deleted from the visible code can still be sitting in the kernel's memory from an earlier run. Build the habit of choosing Kernel, then Restart and Run All, before you share anything with anyone. If it fails, or produces different numbers than before, your notebook depends on state that was never actually written down.

A layout that works well for most analyses has six parts. Title and purpose in a Markdown cell, stating the question you're actually answering. Imports and settings in one cell at the very top, including constants like file paths and thresholds. Load the raw data and do nothing else in that section. Clean it using functions. Analyze with one idea per section, each under its own Markdown heading. And conclusions in plain sentences, backed by real numbers. Keep comments for the why, not the what, and clear or shorten noisy outputs — printing a 10,000-row DataFrame helps absolutely nobody.

To recap: use full, descriptive names and named constants instead of magic numbers. Wrap repeated logic in small functions with docstrings that don't mutate their input. Copy before you modify, to avoid SettingWithCopyWarning. Restart and run all before sharing anything. And structure the notebook top to bottom like a report. Next, we take the next step: moving that reusable logic out of the notebook entirely, into scripts and modules.
